question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
answer:
Counterspell resolves first, and it counters Divination, which never resolves. Divination is currently on the stack underneath Counterspell (since Counterspell was cast in response to it, per [117.7]). When all players pass in succession, the spell on top of the stack resolves ([608.1], [405.5], [117.4]) — that's Counterspell, not Divination.

When Counterspell resolves, it counters its target, Divination: Divination is removed from the stack, it doesn't resolve, and none of its effects occur ([701.6a]). So no cards get drawn. Divination is then put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based result of being countered ([701.6a]), and the caster of Divination does not get a refund of the {2}{U} they spent to cast it ([701.6b]).

After Counterspell finishes resolving (going through the resolution steps in [608.2a]–[608.2n], then being put into its owner's graveyard per [608.2n]), Divination is simply gone from the stack because it was countered — it does not get a separate resolution step of its own. The only way Divination itself would 'resolve' is if it were still on top of the stack when players passed again, but it's not; it left the stack as a result of Counterspell's effect.

This answer assumes the two-player framing implicit in your question ("when everyone passes"); in a multiplayer game with teams, the same resolution order applies, but priority passing works team-by-team rather than player-by-player ([805.5b]) — the outcome for Counterspell and Divination is unchanged either way.

question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?

question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
answer:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers when the cascaded noncreature spell is cast, and that prowess trigger resolves *before* the cascaded spell resolves — it goes on the stack directly on top of the spell that caused it.

Here's the sequence: You cast Shardless Agent, which triggers its cascade ability [603.1]. That cascade ability goes on the stack above Shardless Agent and resolves before Shardless Agent does [Shardless Agent ruling #1]. When cascade resolves, you exile cards until you hit an eligible nonland card and then cast it (this is a genuine 'cast a spell' action, per rule 601.2i, casting includes putting the spell on the stack and paying costs, and any abilities that trigger when a spell is cast trigger 'at this time'). Since that cascaded card is noncreature, Monastery Swiftspear's prowess ability triggers on this cast [702.108a]. Per the Monastery Swiftspear rulings, prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger and resolves before that spell [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2, Monastery Swiftspear ruling #0].

So the final stack order (top to bottom) ends up being: prowess trigger, the cascaded noncreature spell, Shardless Agent. Prowess resolves first (Monastery Swiftspear becomes +1/+1 until end of turn), then the cascaded spell resolves, and finally Shardless Agent itself resolves. Note that even if the cascaded spell were later countered, the prowess trigger would still resolve independently, since once a triggered ability triggers it's no longer connected to the spell that caused it [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #3].

This assumes the cascaded card found is in fact a noncreature spell (if it were a creature spell, or if it had the creature type among others, prowess would not trigger at all, per Monastery Swiftspear ruling #1).

question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
answer:
Yes — Grizzly Bears (a 2/2 creature) will already have died as a state-based action before Lightning Bolt even resolves, in fact before Lightning Bolt could be cast at all in the normal sequence of events.

Here's why: 2 damage marked on a creature with toughness 2 counts as lethal damage, because lethal damage means the total damage marked is greater than or equal to toughness [120.6][302.7]. Whenever any player would receive priority, the game first checks state-based actions, and this happens automatically and repeatedly until none remain before that player gets priority [117.5][704.1][704.2]. So as soon as that 2 damage was marked on Grizzly Bears, the very next time any player would have gotten priority, Grizzly Bears would have been destroyed by state-based actions — this happens before anyone can even cast a spell, since casting a spell requires having priority [117.1][117.5].

This means that under the normal timing (damage was marked on Grizzly Bears at some earlier point, priority was subsequently passed around, and only then did you cast Lightning Bolt), Grizzly Bears would already be in its owner's graveyard by the time you cast Lightning Bolt — you could not even legally target it with Lightning Bolt, since it wouldn't be on the battlefield anymore.

The only way this wouldn't be the case is if the 2 damage was marked and Lightning Bolt was cast in response to the very same event before any player got priority in between (an unusual and specific timing) — but as a general matter, state-based actions check for lethal damage before any spell involving that creature could even be cast, not just before it resolves. Note that even when Lightning Bolt's 3 damage does eventually get applied to a creature, damage itself never directly destroys anything — it's the state-based action that does so afterward [120.5].

question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
answer:
Both triggers actually happen at the exact same instant — the moment your upkeep step begins — but who gets to decide the stacking order is you, the active player, and you put your ability on the stack first, meaning your opponent's ability (put on second) ends up resolving before Phyrexian Arena's ability.

Timing: Per rule [603.2b] and [500.6], any ability that triggers "at the beginning of" a step or phase triggers the instant that step begins — that's the trigger event itself, which is separate from actually being placed on the stack. The upkeep step has no turn-based actions [503.1a][503.1], so as soon as your upkeep begins, both your Phyrexian Arena's ability ("At the beginning of your upkeep, you draw a card and you lose 1 life" — Phyrexian Arena) and your opponent's beginning-of-upkeep ability trigger simultaneously. They aren't put on the stack yet, though — that happens "the next time a player would receive priority" [603.3b], which in the upkeep step is when the active player (you) is about to receive priority [503.1a][117.3a].

Order of stacking: Because two abilities triggered before anyone got priority, rule [603.3b] and the underlying APNAP rule [101.4] apply: the active player (you, since it's your upkeep) puts any triggered abilities you control onto the stack first, then the next player in turn order (here, your opponent, as the nonactive player) puts their triggered ability on the stack. Since the stack resolves last-in-first-out, your opponent's ability — placed on top after yours — resolves first, and Phyrexian Arena's trigger resolves second. Only after both abilities are on the stack do you, the active player, actually receive priority [117.3a].

One important caveat about the scenario itself: an ability worded "at the beginning of your upkeep" only triggers during its controller's own upkeep. If your opponent's ability is written that way, it would not trigger during your upkeep at all — it would trigger only on their own upkeep step. For both abilities to trigger together during your upkeep, your opponent's ability would need to be worded to trigger on your upkeep specifically (e.g., "at the beginning of each upkeep" or "at the beginning of each opponent's upkeep"). Assuming that's the case here, the APNAP-based stacking order above is what applies.

This answer is framed for a two-player game. In a multiplayer game, the same APNAP rule [101.4] would apply, but instead of just you and one opponent, the active player would place their triggers first, then each remaining nonactive player would place theirs in turn order — so with more than two players, whichever nonactive player is last in turn order would have their ability end up resolving first.

question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
answer:
Only one copy of the sorcery ends up in your hand—the original card—not two.

Here's why: Buyback (rule 702.27a) means "If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner's hand instead of into that player's graveyard as it resolves." You paid the buyback cost for the original sorcery, so when the original resolves, that physical card is returned to your hand as normal.

When you cast Fork targeting that sorcery on the stack, Fork creates a copy of the spell per rule 707.10, which states a copy "copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs." So the copy is treated as if buyback was also paid for it, and it would also try to return to a hand instead of going to the graveyard as it resolves. However, per Fork ruling #8, "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you." This is because a copy of a spell is not an actual card—there's no physical card object representing it on the stack (Fork ruling #10)—so there's nothing to put into your hand when the copy's 'return to hand' instruction tries to apply. The copy simply ceases to exist once it finishes resolving.

So the net result: you get one physical card back in hand (the original sorcery, thanks to its paid buyback cost) and the Fork copy vanishes with no card to give you, and the Fork card itself goes to your graveyard.

question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
answer:
No, you do not get a token. Lightning Bolt is an instant card, and even though it died as a face-down manifested permanent, the card that gets exiled with Mimic Vat is the actual Lightning Bolt card (an instant). Mimic Vat's copy ability, "Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact," can only produce a token if the exiled card is a permanent card — you cannot create a token copy of a nonpermanent card like an instant or sorcery. This exact scenario is addressed directly: [Mimic Vat ruling #0] states that if the creature that dies is an instant or sorcery card that's been manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled, and "You can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card. No token is created in this case." This is also consistent with [Mimic Vat ruling #6], which notes that if no (valid) card is exiled at the time the ability resolves, no token is created, and with [Mimic Vat ruling #4], which confirms the token is based on whatever is exiled at resolution time. So when you activate the {3}, {T} ability and it resolves with the manifested Lightning Bolt card exiled, no token is created at all — the ability simply fizzles on the token-creation part.

question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
answer:
Yes, both exiled creatures return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Fiend Hunter's two abilities are linked (per rule 607.2a/406.6): the enters-the-battlefield ability exiles a creature, and the leaves-the-battlefield ability returns "the exiled card." When Lithoform Engine copies the enters-the-battlefield trigger and you choose a new target, the copy is still linked to the same leaves-the-battlefield ability — Lithoform Engine's own ruling confirms that copies of a linked ability remain linked to the second ability in the pair, and specifically gives this exact Fiend Hunter scenario as an example where both exiled creatures return. So Fiend Hunter's leaves-the-battlefield trigger will return both creatures — the one exiled by the original resolution of the enters-the-battlefield ability and the one exiled by Lithoform Engine's copy — to the battlefield under their owners' control. question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
answer:
No. The exiled creature stays exiled and does not return to the battlefield when your Banishing Light phases out.

Banishing Light's ability exiles a creature "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." Phasing out is explicitly not the same as leaving the battlefield: rule [702.26d] states that phasing doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones, even though it's treated as though it isn't on the battlefield while phased out. Teferi's Protection's own rulings confirm this directly for this exact interaction: "Any one-shot effects that are waiting 'until [this] leaves the battlefield,' such as that of Banishing Light, won't happen when a permanent phases out" [Teferi's Protection ruling #21], and "Phasing out doesn't cause any 'leaves the battlefield' abilities to trigger" [Teferi's Protection ruling #17].

So when your Banishing Light phases out (along with your other permanents) from casting Teferi's Protection, the opponent's creature simply remains exiled. When Banishing Light later phases back in (before you untap during your untap step), it's treated as though it never left, so nothing has triggered to return the creature — it stays exiled under Banishing Light's ongoing effect. This is the same for two-player and multiplayer games, since the underlying phasing rule [702.26d] doesn't depend on player count.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
answer:
Yes—your opponent's Counterspell CAN legally target Emrakul, the Promised End, and even if it resolves and counters Emrakul, you still gain control of your opponent's next turn.

Here's why targeting works: Emrakul, the Promised End's protection from instants is a static ability of the permanent, and protection abilities (like all abilities of a permanent other than the stated exceptions) only function while Emrakul is on the battlefield (rule 113.6g). While Emrakul, the Promised End is still a spell on the stack, protection from instants does nothing to prevent it from being targeted — this is confirmed directly by [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2], which states protection only applies on the battlefield and that Emrakul 'may be the target of a spell that targets it while on the stack, such as Syncopate.' Counterspell works the same way here: it can legally target the Emrakul spell.

Now for what happens when Counterspell resolves and counters it: the triggered ability 'When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn' is a separate object from the Emrakul spell itself. It triggered when you cast Emrakul and was put on the stack above the spell as its own triggered-ability object (rule 603.1a). Per rule 113.9, 'Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, and therefore can't be countered by anything that counters only spells.' Counterspell's text is 'Counter target spell' — it can only target and counter the Emrakul spell object, not the triggered ability. So even though your opponent's Counterspell successfully counters the Emrakul, the Promised End spell (putting it into your graveyard as the final part of Counterspell's resolution, per rule 608.2n), the triggered ability is unaffected and still resolves on its own turn on the stack, giving you control of your opponent's next turn and setting up the extra turn for them afterward, exactly as normal (this matches how [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1] and [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #16] describe the ability working independently).

One timing note: I'm assuming the sequence is cast Emrakul → trigger goes on the stack → in response, opponent casts Counterspell targeting the Emrakul spell (which is still lower on the stack). If your opponent instead tried to counter the triggered ability itself, Counterspell couldn't even legally target it, since Counterspell only counters spells, not abilities.

question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
answer:
Yes, it's a legal cascade hit as long as your cascading spell's mana value is greater than 2 - and whether you can cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free depends on your cascading spell's mana value being at least 8.

Here's why. Cascade (rule [702.85a]) exiles cards from the top of your library until you hit a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascading spell's mana value. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card, and while it's sitting in your library/exile (not on the stack), it has one single mana value - 2, the mana value of its front face, Valki, God of Lies (per the card data). So the hit is legal only if your cascading spell's mana value is greater than 2.

Once you've hit it, cascade lets you cast 'that card' from exile. Since Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is exiled face up by default (exiled cards are kept face up per [406.3b], so you can see both faces), and effects that let you cast a card from among exiled cards let you choose either face of a modal double-faced card that fits the effect's criteria (Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16), you may choose to cast either Valki, God of Lies or the back face, Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor.

The catch is cascade's second condition: you may cast the card for free 'if the resulting spell's mana value is less than this spell's mana value' [702.85a]. The special rule that lets a double-faced spell's mana value be calculated from its front face's mana cost while cast 'transformed' or 'converted' applies only to nonmodal double-faced cards [712.8c], [712.8e] - Valki//Tibalt is a modal double-faced card, so that carve-out doesn't apply. If you cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face, the resulting spell is evaluated using Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor's own printed cost, {5}{B}{R}, which is mana value 7. So to cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor for free off cascade, your cascading spell's mana value must be 8 or higher. If your cascading spell's mana value is anywhere from 3 through 7, the hit is still legal (since 2 is less than that), but only casting the Valki, God of Lies face (mana value 2) would satisfy cascade's 'resulting spell's mana value is less' requirement - casting Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor wouldn't be allowed for free in that range.

question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
Control: You control only ONE of your opponent's turns, not two. Copy count for Emrakul, the Promised End: yes, you get a real second Emrakul, the Promised End on the battlefield (a token copy). Casting-trigger count: no, copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself does NOT give you a second "when you cast this spell" trigger.

Here's why. Emrakul, the Promised End's triggered ability reads "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." When Lithoform Engine's first ability ("{2}, {T}: Copy target activated or triggered ability you control") copies that trigger, the copy is put directly onto the stack as a new instance of the same triggered ability [707.10]. So you now have two separate resolutions of "gain control of target opponent's next turn, then that player gets an extra turn," both targeting the same opponent. Per [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14], "Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works... each ability's effect will create an extra turn." Both instances are aimed at the same upcoming "next turn" of that opponent, so the two control-changing effects overwrite each other and you end up actually controlling that single next turn only once — you don't get to control it "twice" or control two different turns from this. However, each of the two resolved abilities still independently spawns its own "after that turn, take an extra turn" delayed effect, so your opponent will take two extra turns after the controlled turn (extra turns for the same player are added one at a time per [500.7]); you do not automatically control those extra turns unless some other effect targets them too.

For the second copy: Lithoform Engine's third ability ("{4}, {T}: Copy target permanent spell you control") copies the Emrakul, the Promised End spell itself while it's still on the stack. As that copy resolves, "A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. The token has the characteristics of the spell that became that token" [111.13]. So yes, you get a genuine second Emrakul, the Promised End — a 13/13 flying, trample, protection-from-instants token — entering the battlefield.

But this does not generate a second "gain control of a turn" trigger. The Emrakul, the Promised End ability that grants control triggers on "when you cast this spell," and a copy created by Lithoform Engine is never cast — "a copy of a spell isn't cast" [707.10], and Lithoform Engine's own ruling confirms "Creating the copy won't cause abilities that trigger when a player casts a spell or activates an ability to trigger" [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. So the token copy of Emrakul, the Promised End does not re-trigger the control-a-turn ability; only the original cast trigger and the Lithoform Engine copy of that trigger (the first thing you did) count toward the control/extra-turn math above.

This analysis is the same whether you're playing two-player or multiplayer, since only a single targeted opponent is involved and the extra turns are simply added one at a time for that one player [500.7]; the multiplayer-specific rules about team turns or Grand Melee turn order [805.8], [807.4] and APNAP ordering among multiple players [101.4] would only come into play if these effects targeted or affected more than one opponent's turns simultaneously, which isn't the case here.

question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
answer:
Yes, you get two tokens. Lithoform Engine's first ability copies target activated ability you control, putting another instance of that ability onto the stack (Lithoform Engine ruling #3): "Lithoform Engine's first ability targets an activated or triggered ability that is on the stack and creates another instance of that ability on the stack. It doesn't cause any object to gain an ability." A copy of an ability copies the characteristics and decisions made for it, but choices normally made on resolution are not copied [707.10b]. Mimic Vat's activated ability, "Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact. It gains haste. Exile it at the beginning of the next end step," doesn't target the exiled card — instead, per Mimic Vat ruling #4, the token created will be a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat *at the time the ability resolves*. So when the original activated ability and the Lithoform Engine copy of it both resolve (the copy resolves first, since it was put on the stack after the original), each one independently checks what's exiled with Mimic Vat and creates its own token copy of that card. Since the imprinted creature card is still exiled with Mimic Vat when each resolves (nothing removes it in between), each resolution creates a separate token — giving you two token copies of the imprinted creature, each with haste, each exiled at the beginning of the next end step (Mimic Vat's printed text). This assumes the two resolutions happen in immediate succession with nothing removing the exiled card between them; if something caused the card to leave exile after the first token was made but before the second ability resolved, the second copy would fail to make a token (per Mimic Vat ruling #6, no card exiled means no token).

question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
With X=0, Awaken the Woods costs {1}{G}{G} (1 generic mana + 2 green mana, i.e. 3 mana total) and you get zero Forest Dryad tokens — you pay Trinisphere's full tax for nothing. You should choose X=2 instead, which also costs {1}{G}{G} but gives you 2 tokens for the same price; that's the most value you can get at the minimum 3-mana price Trinisphere forces.

Why this happens: Awaken the Woods' mana cost is {X}{G}{G} [Awaken the Woods]. To determine what you actually pay, you build the total cost in the order Trinisphere's ruling specifies: start with the mana cost as cast (with your chosen X), apply cost increases, then apply cost reductions, and only then apply Trinisphere's effect if what remains is under three mana [Trinisphere ruling #0]. Under rule 601.2f, a cost reduction can lower the generic-mana part of a cost but can never push it below {0} [601.2f].

- X=0: the spell's cost is just {G}{G} (X contributes {0} generic). Your -{1}-to-green-spells reducer has nothing left to reduce, so the cost stays {G}{G} (2 mana). Since that's less than three mana, Trinisphere raises it back up to three mana total, giving {1}{G}{G}. You paid 3 mana and get 0 tokens (X is locked in at 0 per 601.2b/107.3a, so you still create X=0 tokens).
- X=1: the {X} generic slot is {1}, your reducer knocks it to {0}, leaving {G}{G} again — under three mana, so Trinisphere again pads it to {1}{G}{G} (3 mana). You'd pay the same 3 mana for only 1 token.
- X=2: the {X} slot is {2}, your reducer knocks it to {1}, leaving {1}{G}{G} — that's already 3 mana total, so Trinisphere's minimum is already satisfied and doesn't add anything. You pay {1}{G}{G} (3 mana) and get 2 tokens.

So X=2 is the smallest value at which your cost reducer actually 'counts' against Trinisphere's floor instead of being wasted; for the same 3 mana you get twice the tokens of the X=0 line. Going higher than X=2 (X=3, X=4, ...) costs {X-1}{G}{G} each time — i.e., every point of X above 2 costs exactly 1 more generic mana for 1 more token — so if you have more mana available, pushing X higher is strictly efficient too. X=0 and X=1 are simply the two worst options since Trinisphere charges the same 3-mana minimum for less (or no) payoff.

Note: the value of X is announced and locked in when you cast the spell (rule 601.2b), and while the spell is on the stack that announced value is what X equals for the spell's text and its cost (rule 107.3a) — you can't change your mind about X after seeing Trinisphere's effect apply, so you need to choose X up front knowing this tax structure.

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes. Because Grist, the Hunger Tide is currently in your graveyard, it is (per Grist, the Hunger Tide's own text and Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1) a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect while off the battlefield, so it satisfies Animate Dead's enchant requirement of "creature card in a graveyard." You may cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard.

Here's what happens when Animate Dead resolves, per its own printed text and Animate Dead ruling #1: Animate Dead enters attached to the Grist, the Hunger Tide card in the graveyard, loses the "enchant creature card in a graveyard" text and gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," then returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and re-attaches itself to the returned Grist, the Hunger Tide (which is a new object per rule 400.7, since anything moving zones becomes a new object).

Once Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield, it stops being a creature — Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1 explicitly says that once it enters the battlefield it is no longer a creature and is just a planeswalker. This means Animate Dead's "Enchanted creature gets -1/-0" has no effect on it, because Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature while on the battlefield (there's no power/toughness to modify). Grist, the Hunger Tide will simply be a planeswalker with 3 starting loyalty under your control, and Animate Dead's own text overrides how enchant-a-creature-card Auras normally work — this is a case of card text taking precedence over the general rule that an Aura's target type must match the permanent it ends up on.

If Animate Dead is ever destroyed, countered from a static-ability standpoint, or otherwise leaves the battlefield, its delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it") still refers to the specific object that Animate Dead returned — i.e., the Grist, the Hunger Tide planeswalker — so you would still have to sacrifice it even though it is no longer a creature type at that time; the ability's "that creature" wording names the specific returned object rather than re-checking its current card type. Also note that per Animate Dead ruling #2, once Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield, Animate Dead can never move to enchant any other permanent.

One more consequence worth flagging: while Grist, the Hunger Tide sits in the graveyard as a creature card, it also counts toward the creature-card count for Grist, the Hunger Tide's own −5 loyalty ability if another Grist, the Hunger Tide's ability resolves while this one is in the graveyard (Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #4), though that's incidental to the Animate Dead interaction itself.

question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
answer:
Yes, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters through the whole sequence, but no, Doubling Season does not double them.

Skullbriar's own printed text says: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." This overrides the normal rule that counters cease to exist when an object changes zones (rule [122.2], object becomes a new object with no memory of the old one under [400.7]). Since the graveyard, the command zone, the stack, and the battlefield are all zones other than hand or library, the four +1/+1 counters survive every step: battlefield → graveyard (when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies), graveyard → command zone (moving your commander there under [903.9a], or via the replacement effect in [903.9b] if you choose to redirect it straight from dying into the command zone instead), command zone → stack (when you recast it), and stack → battlefield (when it resolves and enters again). Note that each of these zone changes technically makes Skullbriar, the Walking Grave a "new object" ([400.7], and specifically [400.10] for an object put into the command zone again), but its own ability is what re-attaches the same number and kinds of counters each time, per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] (it retains all counters, not just +1/+1 ones).

Doubling Season will NOT double these counters. Doubling Season's second ability only doubles counters that an effect "would put" onto a permanent you control, which includes permanents that enter the battlefield with counters. But [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] explicitly states that the counters which remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones aren't "placed" on it — they simply remain — so Doubling Season's doubling effect does not apply to them. So when you recast Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it re-enters the battlefield still carrying exactly four +1/+1 counters, not eight.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players at the table — the commander zone-change rules in [903.9a]/[903.9b] and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own counter-retention text work the same whether it's a two-player or multiplayer Commander game.

question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
answer:
No, you do not lose the game. Final Fortune's delayed triggered ability only triggers "at the beginning of that turn's end step," but activating Sundial of the Infinite's ability ends the extra turn before the end step ever begins. Because the current step/phase ends and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, the end step of that turn is skipped entirely, and per rule [724.1e], "'at the beginning of the end step' triggered abilities don't trigger because the end step is skipped." This is confirmed directly by [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1]: activating the ability before the end step means any "at the beginning of the end step" triggers won't get a chance to trigger that turn.

The key wrinkle is that Final Fortune's delayed trigger is worded to reference a specific turn's end step ("that turn's end step" — the extra turn granted by Final Fortune), not a recurring ability. Since that particular end step never occurs (it's skipped, not merely postponed), the trigger condition is never met for that turn, and the turn itself is already over once Sundial of the Infinite resolves per [724.1d] (skip straight to cleanup). So there is no later end step for that specific delayed trigger to attach to — it simply never fires, and Sundial of the Infinite's own text explicitly overrides the normal expectation that end-of-turn effects happen, since ending the turn this way (per [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #4]) skips straight past the end step to cleanup with no priority and no triggered abilities going on the stack from that skipped step.

This is analogous in spirit to [Final Fortune ruling #1], which notes that if you skip the extra turn entirely, you don't lose — here you're not skipping the whole turn, but you are skipping the specific step (the end step) that the loss condition is tied to, which produces the same practical result: no loss.

This answer doesn't depend on player count, since it concerns a single player's own extra turn and its steps, not turn order among multiple players.

question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
answer:
You choose what Clone copies during the resolution of the Clone spell itself, as it enters the battlefield — not as a separate ability that opponents get to respond to.

Rule [707.5] explains that a permanent that enters the battlefield "as a copy" of another object becomes that copy right as it enters — it doesn't enter first and then become a copy afterward. This means the copy-choice is a replacement effect tied to the entering-the-battlefield event, resolved as part of Clone's spell resolving, not a separate triggered or activated ability that goes on the stack. Since it never goes on the stack, no player gets priority specifically over that choice, so your opponent cannot respond to it directly.

Additionally, per [Clone ruling #0], Clone's ability doesn't target the chosen creature at all — there's no targeting step for anyone to respond to (e.g., no way to fizzle it via Hexproof or a "protection from targeting" effect), and no target is locked in during the casting/announcement steps of casting Clone under [601.2c].

You may only choose a creature that is already on the battlefield at the moment Clone enters — per [Clone ruling #2], if another creature would enter the battlefield simultaneously with Clone, Clone cannot copy it, since the ability is being applied as it itself enters. You are also allowed to choose not to copy anything, per [Clone ruling #5], in which case Clone is just a 0/0 Shapeshifter (and dies to state-based actions).

What your opponent *can* do is act earlier: while Clone is still a spell on the stack (before it resolves), your opponent has priority to cast instants or activate abilities — for example, to remove the creature they don't want you to copy from the battlefield, or to add/alter a creature — since your choice is locked in only when Clone actually enters and is limited to creatures on the battlefield at that time. They cannot, however, respond *to the choice itself* once Clone starts resolving.

This analysis holds in both two-player and multiplayer games, since the copy-choice is not a triggered or activated ability subject to APNAP ordering (rule [101.4]) — it's a replacement effect applied unilaterally by Clone's controller as it enters the battlefield, regardless of how many players are at the table.

question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
answer:
You get 3 lands total from that single Flooded Strand activation. Activating Flooded Strand's ability ("{T}, Pay 1 life, Sacrifice this land: Search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle.") puts that activated ability on the stack once. Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability, activated with X=2, targets that ability on the stack and creates 2 additional copies of it (per [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6], which states Gogo's ability "creates one or more additional instances of that ability on the stack"). That means there are now 3 total instances of Flooded Strand's ability on the stack: the original plus the 2 copies. Since a copy of an activated ability isn't itself activated (rule [707.10b]), none of the copies need to pay Flooded Strand's tap/life/sacrifice costs again — those costs were already paid once, for the original activation. Each of the 3 instances resolves independently and performs the full effect: search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle. So you end up putting 3 lands onto the battlefield from that one Flooded Strand, even though the land itself is sacrificed only once. Note that the source of each copied ability remains Flooded Strand itself, per [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9], so all three searches are attributed to the same source card.
